ui.alert.title: {name}!
ui.alert.toll: Estimated toll so far: {dead}. It is an estimate — for a building that came down the game works out how many did not get out.
ui.alert.body.fire: The city is on fire. Flames spread to neighbouring tiles and only a road, water or a bulldozed firebreak will stop them. Fire brigades help only where they reach.
ui.alert.body.wildfire: The forest is burning. There is time to cut a break before the fire reaches the buildings — after that it is too late.
ui.alert.body.flood: Water is rising and flooding the lowland. Flooded buildings decay until it recedes. A raised bank holds it back.
ui.alert.body.tornado: A tornado is crossing the city, taking whatever stands in its way. It cannot be stopped, only cleaned up after.
ui.alert.body.earthquake: An earthquake. Buildings collapse or drop a level, roads and pipes crack. Tall blocks take it better than low ones.
ui.alert.body.explosion: An explosion. The surroundings are flattened and burning.
ui.alert.body.industrialAccident: An industrial accident. Blast and fire have hit the surrounding area.
ui.alert.body.pileup: A pile-up is blocking the road. Traffic around it is stuck until it is cleared.
ui.alert.body.strike: A strike in the district. Services there are down and happiness falls until conditions improve. An unresolved strike can grow into a riot.
ui.alert.body.riot: Civil unrest. The district is out of control, land value is falling and the police have their hands full.
ui.alert.body.gangWar: A gang war. Nothing is destroyed, but the district gets permanently worse — crime up, land value down.
ui.alert.body.blackout: A blackout. Power plants have dropped out and without power the services are down too, so the risk of everything else has jumped.
ui.alert.body.epidemic: An epidemic. Disease is spreading among the residents and people are dying. Only enough health coverage will stop it.
ui.alert.body.chemicalSpill: A chemical spill. The waterworks is out and the surroundings stay poisoned even after the leak ends.
ui.alert.body.landslide: A landslide. The slope gave way and took what stood on it.

ui.help.problem.waste.title: Waste and sewage cannot keep up
ui.help.problem.waste.cause: Whatever the landfill, incinerator and treatment plant cannot handle spreads into pollution evenly across the whole map, not just around the city. It is the single largest source of smog in the game and it cannot be found on the map, because it has no centre.
ui.help.problem.waste.fix: Add an incinerator, a landfill or a treatment plant. Capacity against demand is in the top bar next to power and reads the same way: on the left what you can handle, on the right what the city needs.
ui.help.problem.growth.title: Zones sit there and nothing grows
ui.help.problem.growth.cause: A marked zone is a plan, not a building. Until a plot meets everything at once - a road within two tiles, water, power, level ground and positive demand - nothing is built on it, and the game says nothing.
ui.help.problem.growth.fix: Click an empty plot inside the zone: the plot card says exactly what is missing. Most often it is water or the distance to a road.

ui.alert.story.fire:
Fire. Flames have broken through the windows into the street and smoke is creeping under the neighbours’ doors. The brigade is on its way, but until it arrives the fire spreads — and what burns is not repaired, it is demolished.

Check whether that quarter has a fire station within reach at all.
ui.alert.story.wildfire:
The woods are burning. Wind is driving the fire up the slope and embers are landing where we expected quiet. The smoke is visible across the whole city.

Until the flames reach bare ground or water, they will not stop on their own.
ui.alert.story.flood:
The water has risen. Low streets are under the surface, ground floors are filling and nothing gets through. The drains cannot cope.

When it falls there will be mud, mould and a bill. Building on the flood plain was always a bet.
ui.alert.story.tornado:
A tornado came through. In a few minutes it took roofs, snapped trees and left a strip you can see from the far side of town.

What stood in its way no longer stands. The rest was lucky.
ui.alert.story.earthquake:
The whole city shook. The asphalt has cracked, balconies came off the facades and people are standing outside looking at their houses.

Older buildings may not have taken it. Someone will have to count what can be saved.
ui.alert.story.explosion:
An explosion. The ground floor is gone, there is a hole where a wall was and glass reached across the street. They heard it in the next quarter.

Everything within the radius took it head on. The rest took a fright.
ui.alert.story.industrialAccident:
An accident at the works. The hall roof is open, steam is escaping from the pipework and what used to be a tank is lying in the yard.

Production has stopped and the neighbourhood pays in health and in land value. Industry next to housing always has this catch.
ui.alert.story.pileup:
A pile-up. Vehicles are blocking both lanes and traffic around it is at a standstill. Until it is cleared, everyone is looking for a way round.

One overloaded junction can stop half a city. Perhaps it is time for a wider road.
ui.alert.story.strike:
A strike. The depot is shut, the trams are parked in a row and nobody is going anywhere. People are getting to work however they can.

While it lasts, the city has no transit at all. And happiness falls faster than takings.
ui.alert.story.riot:
Riots. Bins are burning in the streets, shop windows are broken and people are staying in. This did not fall out of the sky — it had been hanging in the air.

An unhappy city speaks up sooner or later. This is the later.
ui.alert.story.gangWar:
A gang war. There was shooting in the side streets; by morning there is a burnt-out car and nobody saw anything.

Where policing and work are missing, this moves in. The quarter will remember it for a long time.
ui.alert.story.blackout:
A blackout. The whole quarter is dark, lifts have stopped, fridges are thawing and nothing works in the shops.

The grid could not carry what was asked of it. Either add supply or cut demand — otherwise another one is coming.
ui.alert.story.epidemic:
An epidemic. Ambulances are queuing outside the hospital, a white tent has gone up on the lawn and people only go out when they must.

A city with few doctors and high density pays twice: first in health, then in mood.
ui.alert.story.chemicalSpill:
A chemical spill. An overturned tanker has emptied onto the road and from there into the drain. You can smell it three streets away.

The water here is unusable until it is cleaned up. And the works that draws from it will not deliver a drop.
ui.alert.story.landslide:
A landslide. The slope tore away and lay down across the road, together with the trees and a piece of the garden above it. Nothing gets through.

Hills look nice on the map. Cut into them and they occasionally answer back.
ui.parcel.risk: Warning: this district is at risk of {name}.
error.needsRoadFar: It must touch a road and there is none anywhere near. Run one here first.
ui.help.buildings.title: Buildings
ui.help.buildings.lead: Everything you can build, with the numbers straight from the rules. Change the balance and this list changes with it.
ui.help.problems.title: Problems
ui.help.problems.lead: What goes wrong in a city, why it happens and what to do about it. The messages the game shows on a parcel are listed here too.
ui.help.fact.slope: Takes a slope, no levelling needed
ui.help.fact.waterRange: Extends the water network by tiles
ui.help.problem.noZone.title: The parcel is not zoned
ui.help.problem.noZone.cause: Residents build the houses, but only where you let them. Bare grass stays grass even with a road, water and power next to it.
ui.help.problem.noZone.fix: Mark a zone — residential, commercial or industrial. A zone is a plan, not a building: it costs nothing but the levelling under it.
ui.help.problem.noDemand.title: No demand
ui.help.problem.noDemand.cause: The R/C/I bars at the top say what the city is hungry for. Homes need jobs, shops need customers, industry needs buyers. High taxes push demand down.
ui.help.problem.noDemand.fix: Zone whatever is short and balance the other side: add jobs to a housing district, housing to an industrial one. If nothing wants to grow, try a lower tax.
ui.help.problem.tooFarFromRoad.title: Too far from a road
ui.help.problem.tooFarFromRoad.cause: A house wants a road at most two tiles away. Beyond that the parcel never grows, however good it looks otherwise.
ui.help.problem.tooFarFromRoad.fix: Run a street to the parcel. It does not have to be an avenue — the cheapest road carries the same reach.
ui.help.problem.zoneTooSmall.title: The zone is too shallow
ui.help.problem.zoneTooSmall.cause: A building has a footprint and has to fit inside the zone. A 2×2 factory never fits a single strip along a road.
ui.help.problem.zoneTooSmall.fix: Mark at least two rows side by side; three for industry and large buildings.
ui.help.problem.needsWater.title: No water
ui.help.problem.needsWater.cause: Water flows only through pipes and only 24 tiles from the waterworks. A lone pipe under a house is a hole in the ground; the network has to be continuous back to the source.
ui.help.problem.needsWater.fix: Lay pipes in the underground view and follow the roads to the waterworks. If the district is beyond the reach, add a pump station at the edge of the watered area.
ui.help.problem.needsPower.title: No power
ui.help.problem.needsPower.cause: Power flows along roads and through buildings from the plant. An unpowered building also pays no tax, so an outage costs more than it looks.
ui.help.problem.needsPower.fix: Build a plant and join it to the district with a road — there are no separate power lines, so anything not linked by roads or buildings stays dark. Watch the reserve: when demand catches up with output, outages begin.
ui.help.problem.rubble.title: Rubble
ui.help.problem.rubble.cause: Left by a disaster or by demolition. It blocks the parcel for good — nothing grows there and you cannot build or lay pipes across it.
ui.help.problem.rubble.fix: Clear it with the bulldozer. It costs money and after a big disaster it is the first spending that pays off.
ui.help.problem.bankrupt.title: In the red
ui.help.problem.bankrupt.cause: Negative funds stop growth in the whole city, not just where the loss is. It is the hardest stop in the game and cities often never recover.
ui.help.problem.bankrupt.fix: Raise taxes, cut service funding, demolish what the city cannot carry, and borrow — but a loan is derived from income, so with no income there is none.
ui.help.problem.noDefinition.title: Nothing to build
ui.help.problem.noDefinition.cause: The content has no building for this zone at all. Vanilla never hits this; a mod that adds a zone without buildings does.
ui.help.problem.noDefinition.fix: Add a building of the matching category to the content, or drop the zone.
ui.help.problem.notFlat.title: A slope
ui.help.problem.notFlat.cause: Most buildings want a flat parcel. Levelling happens automatically and is added to the price; what cannot be levelled without breaking the road next to it is refused.
ui.help.problem.notFlat.fix: Level the parcel with the terrain tool, or build something that takes a slope — a park sits on a hill as it is.
ui.help.problem.terrain.title: Wrong surface
ui.help.problem.terrain.cause: Nothing is built on rock, marsh or forest. Forest also absorbs pollution, so there is no point felling it for nothing.
ui.help.problem.terrain.fix: The bulldozer clears forest, quarries rock and fills marsh — each at its own price. Or simply build elsewhere.
ui.help.problem.abandoned.title: The house decayed
ui.help.problem.abandoned.cause: Too long without water or power, or in a district that is too unhappy. The empty house then stands as a ruin, spoils the area and pays nothing.
ui.help.problem.abandoned.fix: Bring water and power, spread the services fairly and demolish the ruin — a new house grows there once there is demand.
ui.help.problem.pollution.title: Pollution
ui.help.problem.pollution.cause: Industry, power plants and above all landfills smoke. Worst of all is unhandled waste and sewage: those spread evenly across the whole map, not just around the city. Pollution drags down land value, health and happiness.
ui.help.problem.pollution.fix: Build a landfill or an incinerator for waste and a treatment plant for sewage — the capacity has to match the population. Put the landfill at the edge; it smokes more than a coal plant. Forest absorbs half the smoke around it, so planting it around factories pays.
ui.help.problem.crime.title: Crime
ui.help.problem.crime.cause: It grows where land value is low, houses are poor or abandoned and police coverage is missing. High crime lowers land value further, so it feeds itself.
ui.help.problem.crime.fix: Build police so the radius covers the whole district, clear the ruins and lift land value with parks and services.
ui.help.problem.traffic.title: Congestion
ui.help.problem.traffic.cause: When a road carries more people than it can, a jam forms. It slows commuting, lowers happiness and pileups happen in jams.
ui.help.problem.traffic.fix: Put an avenue or a highway where the traffic is, run public transport and shorten the distances — jobs near homes are the cheapest fix.
ui.help.problem.unhappy.title: Unhappiness
ui.help.problem.unhappy.cause: It adds up from service coverage, taxes, pollution, crime, congestion and recent disasters. An unhappy city grows slower and its houses decay.
ui.help.problem.unhappy.fix: Open the happiness heat map and fix whatever is worst in that district. Coverage and a lower tax work fastest.
ui.help.problem.blackout.title: Blackout
ui.help.problem.blackout.cause: The risk rises once the production reserve falls below a quarter of demand, and a big plant drops out sooner than a small one. The cascade then takes them offline one by one.
ui.help.problem.blackout.fix: Keep a reserve and prefer several smaller plants to one big one. During a blackout build nothing expensive — the city collects no tax meanwhile.
ui.help.problem.noWaterReach.title: Water does not reach
ui.help.problem.noWaterReach.cause: The waterworks pushes water only 24 tiles along the pipes. Beyond that the network is dry even with the works running at full.
ui.help.problem.noWaterReach.fix: Put a pump station on the last watered tile towards the dry district — it adds another twenty tiles of reach. Or add a second waterworks on another shore.
ui.help.problem.fire.title: Fire
ui.help.problem.fire.cause: It starts on its own, after an explosion and after an earthquake. Without a fire station it spreads to the neighbouring tiles as long as there is something to burn.
ui.help.problem.fire.fix: Build fire stations so the radius covers the built-up area. Once it burns, cut a firebreak with the bulldozer — fire does not cross an empty tile.
ui.help.problem.services.title: Missing coverage
ui.help.problem.services.cause: Every service has a radius and a strength. Both fall with the budget: an underfunded service covers less even though the building still stands.
ui.help.problem.services.fix: Build another station closer to the district, or raise that budget. The coverage map shows how far it really reaches.
ui.help.title: Help
ui.help.lead: Zdenalcity has no tutorial. This is where you find out why something will not build, will not grow, or is falling apart.
ui.help.start.title: Before the first house
ui.help.start.body:
A city needs four things, in this order: a road, a zone, water and power. Miss one and nothing grows.

– Build a bit of street. Houses only grow within two tiles of a road.

– Mark a residential zone next to it. A zone is a plan, not a building: people build the houses themselves, if they want to live there.

– Build a water works on the shore (it needs both water and a road) and run pipes from it under the zone. Pipes are laid in the underground view. The water works is what produces water; a pump station only extends the reach of the pipes and supplies nothing on its own.

– Build a power plant and connect it to the zone by road. Power runs along roads and through buildings; there are no other lines, so a district without an unbroken road to a plant stays dark.

Then wait. Game speed is at the top, next to the date.
ui.help.zones.title: Zones and demand
ui.help.zones.body:
Three zones: residential, commercial, industrial. The gauges at the top right say which one is wanted right now.

Positive demand means the zone will fill once you mark it. Negative means there is enough of it: the zone stays empty and you have paid for levelling for nothing.

The demands hold each other up. People want jobs, shops want customers and staff, industry wants somewhere to sell. A city of flats alone stalls on unemployment; a city of factories alone has nobody to staff them.

A zone that will not grow always has a specific reason. Click an empty plot and the card says it on the first line.
ui.help.roads.title: Roads and traffic
ui.help.roads.body:
Three types: street, avenue, highway. They differ in capacity, price and upkeep; a wider road carries more cars but you pay for it every month.

Congestion is not cosmetic. A jammed road cuts job access, and that drags growth and happiness down across the district. The Traffic view shows where it stands still.

Transit takes load off. A stop, a depot and a line between stops move part of the trips off the roads.

Roads are built by dragging. Over water you get a bridge; it costs more and must start on the shore.
ui.help.utilities.title: Water and power
ui.help.utilities.body:
Without water nothing grows and what stands starts to decay. A water works on the shore produces the water and pipes carry it; they are laid in the underground view.

Only a water works produces water. A pump station adds none, it merely extends the reach of the pipes, so a city without a water works stays dry. Pipes have a reach: the further from the source, the weaker the pressure; where water does not arrive, the pipe is drawn dry.

Power runs along roads and through buildings. There are no separate power lines — when a district is dark, what is missing is an unbroken road from a plant, not the plant itself.

A building without power does not work. For services that means no coverage: a fire station without power does not roll out.

One pipe under a single tile of a building is enough, not under all of them. A large building has water as soon as a pipe runs under one corner of its footprint.

Water only travels 24 tiles along the pipes from the waterworks. Beyond that the network is dry even at full production — that is what pump stations are for: put one on the last watered tile towards the dry district and the reach grows by another twenty.

Waste and sewage are not the water network. Whatever a landfill, an incinerator and a treatment plant do not cover spreads as pollution across the whole map, not just around the city. The capacities are in the top bar next to power: Waste, Sewage and Water. They read like power — what you can handle on the left, what the city needs on the right.

A waterworks has a capacity, not just a reach. When the city drinks more than is pumped, the far end of the network runs dry first. A pump station extends the reach but produces no water — that takes another waterworks.

A bridge is built with the road tool but has to start on the bank. A click in open water is refused; set off from land and carry on across.
ui.help.services.title: Services and their reach
ui.help.services.body:
Police, fire, health, schools, parks, culture, community and transit. Each building covers its surroundings up to its reach, weaker the further out.

Reach is measured in tiles and every building lists its own in the catalogue of buildings, which is built from the data and so cannot go stale. The rule holds either way: a service covers a district, not a city.

Turn on a Reach view and you will see a white boundary where the service ends, and a pin with its icon above every station. The thinner line inside separates weak coverage from adequate.

Service funding can be cut. You save money, but reach and strength shrink with it: underfunded firefighters take longer.

Education is not decoration. Besides happiness it unlocks better buildings: offices and shopping centres want coverage 40, high rises and the industrial park 70. Without schools a district never levels up, however good everything else is.

Social is a service class like any other — community centres and social care. It holds happiness up where neither a park nor a police station helps.

Funding changes three things at once: radius, strength and the upkeep you actually pay. Cut to 60 % and you pay 60 % for less cover.

You can also go above a hundred per cent, up to double — useful when the city is burning and the fire service cannot keep up. It is deliberately a bad deal: above a hundred the effect grows by only half the surplus (at 200 % the service covers like 150 %), while the price grows progressively. The step from 190 to 200 % costs twenty times the step from 90 to 100 %, and a doubled budget comes to twelve times the upkeep. It is an emergency lever, not a substitute for a second station.
ui.help.quality.title: Land value, happiness, crime
ui.help.quality.body:
Land value decides how high a district grows. Parks, schools, nearby water and a good outlook raise it; pollution, crime, rubble and ruins drag it down.

Happiness is the average of how it is to live there. An unhappy district empties out and eventually falls apart.

Crime grows where land value is low and police are missing. Ruins and rubble feed it on their own.

All of this has its own heat map under Layers: green is great, red is terrible. The plot card then shows what the number is made of.
ui.help.terrain.title: Terrain
ui.help.terrain.body:
Buildings stand on the level. An uneven plot is levelled by the build itself and added to the price; the plot card tells you in advance.

The Terrain tool raises and lowers corners and levels ground. Levelling takes the height of the tile where the drag started: take a tile, drag, and the surroundings match it.

A road can climb and bank, but not twist. When a change of terrain takes its flat away, it breaks and leaves rubble.

Rock can be quarried, marsh filled and forest cleared: all with the bulldozer and all for money. Until then a forest raises land value and absorbs pollution.

Raising and lowering moves a corner, not a tile — and the neighbouring corners with it, so the ground keeps its one-level step. You see all of it before you click: the corner under the cursor lit fully, the cascade faintly, and the price above the cursor.

Level (F) is the safest tool: it takes the height of the tile where the drag started and pulls the surroundings to it. Fill (G) instead raises the area to the highest corner — a hill becomes a terrace at the top instead of a pit at the bottom.

Plant trees (T) is the opposite of felling. Forest absorbs half the pollution around it and lifts land value; it is the only defence against smoke with no upkeep.
ui.help.money.title: Money
ui.help.money.body:
Income is tax from residential, commercial and industrial zones. A high rate earns now but puts people off; a low one starts growth that pays later.

Spending is upkeep. Every road, pipe and building is paid for monthly: building it is once, having it is forever.

When money runs out you can take a loan or issue bonds. A loan is repaid monthly, a bond comes back whole on its maturity day. A defaulted issue closes the market for a while.

The monthly balance at the top shows income and spending apart. A negative one for long is not a disaster today: it is a disaster in a year.

How much tax? Measurement says 11 to 14 percent is a sound base. A low tax gets growth going but does not feed the city: across a thousand simulated games only a quarter of the cities on about five percent lived a hundred years, against more than three quarters on about seventeen. The price is a smaller city — a high tax slows people moving in.

Since T113 a high rate hurts progressively: up to seven percent it costs exactly the happiness it always did, at twenty it costs twice that. Measured over 311 paired games (same seed, both balances): strategies holding 16 to 18 percent lost 27.5 points of happiness [-39.5, -14.8], while survival and city size did not move. Sitting on a high rate is paid for in mood, not in bankruptcy.

When the monthly balance goes negative, raise the tax before the money runs out. In the red growth stops in the whole city and cities rarely climb back out.
ui.help.disasters.title: Disasters
ui.help.disasters.body:
Natural ones (tornado, earthquake, flood, landslide, wildfire) come regardless of what you built.

Man-made ones the city brings on itself. Fire where flammable buildings have no fire cover; riots and gang wars where crime has no police; a strike in an unhappy district; a pile-up on a jammed junction; accidents in heavy industry; an epidemic in a dense estate without doctors.

The Disaster risk layer shows where it threatens most, and the plot card names what exactly.

While something is running, an icon sits next to the clock. Click it and the report comes back. The bulldozer fights fire: a firebreak is the only active defence you have.

Disasters can be switched off entirely. Disasters menu, toggle at the top.

The disaster card takes you where it hurts, not where the epicentre landed. An earthquake has its epicentre anywhere, wilderness included — the shake spreads across the whole map anyway, so there is nothing to see at the epicentre.

The parcel card line “this district risks…” means that exactly this disaster came out likely there. For a pileup that is usually a jammed junction, for fire flammable buildings with no fire station, for riots crime with no police.
ui.help.controls.title: Controls
ui.help.controls.body:
– The hand drags the map, the wheel zooms.

– Left button builds, dragging paints. Right button opens the card of whatever you point at.

– Clicking a building or plot with the hand opens its breakdown. That is the answer to most questions starting with why.

– The underground view switches to pipes. Tools follow: pipes below, roads above.

– Ghost buildings reveal what is underneath. Trees and boulders can be hidden entirely.

– Game speed is at the top, after the date. Pause is a full state, not an interruption: you can build in it.

– Drag the map with the pan tool and the left button, with the middle button from anywhere, or with space and the left button. The wheel zooms; on touch there are magnifier buttons.

– The R/C/I bars at the top explain themselves on hover. If they look random, the answer is right there.

– The map does not rotate. Every building is drawn from a single angle, so rotating would mean drawing the whole city again from four sides.
ui.help.saving.title: Saving
ui.help.saving.body:
The game saves itself into the browser and the home page then offers to continue. Clearing site data deletes it.

Quick save and load hold one slot in the browser. Save to file makes a .city file you can keep, move elsewhere, or send to the author when something breaks.

A save from a newer version is refused loudly by an older one. An older save is migrated by a newer game itself.

The game also runs as an app: it can be installed to the desktop from the browser and then works offline.
ui.version.dev: Development run — the version shows in a real build.
ui.save.updateHint: Downloads the new build. Your city stays.
ui.save.updating: Loading the new version, your city is saved…
ui.home.share: Send the game to a friend
ui.home.shareNote: The link to the game in one tap.
ui.home.shareText: Try Zdenalcity — an isometric city builder in your browser.
ui.help.transit.title: Public transport
ui.help.transit.body:
A stop is a building, a line is a list of stops and vehicles are a number. No rails and no tunnels are built — tram and metro are abstractions, not track. The metro is a stop with a bigger radius and higher capacity; nothing is dug underground.

Before the first stop you need a depot. Without one the game refuses the stop.

A line runs when it has at least two stops, vehicles, and — for tram and metro — power at the stops. One stop may serve several lines at once.

The run/park button parks the line: vehicles sit in the depot, carry nobody and earn nothing — but pay no upkeep either, and the stops stay. The cross on a stop drops it from the line, clicking its name shows it on the map.

A demolished stop leaves the line on its own. The line keeps running on the rest, and when fewer than two remain it says so.
